# Still Here: Notes on the Oldest Things in the World

Sometime around 12,400 BC, in what is now northeastern Jordan, someone baked bread. We know this because in 2018, archaeologists sifting through the remains of a stone fireplace at a site called Shubayqa 1 found charred crumbs — tiny blackened fragments of flatbread, analyzed under an electron microscope until their ingredients could be named: flour ground from wild wheat and barley, mixed with the pulverized tubers of a wetland sedge. The bread was unleavened, probably cooked on hot stones or in the ashes. And here is the fact that stops you: it was baked more than four thousand years before anyone, anywhere, had planted a field. The people at Shubayqa were hunter-gatherers, Natufians, who hunted gazelle and gathered what the land offered. Agriculture had not been invented. Villages barely existed. Writing was ten thousand years in the future. And yet there was bread.

Think about what that means. Gathering wild grasses seed by seed, grinding them between stones, mashing tubers, mixing, shaping, baking — it is an enormous amount of labor for a band of people who carried everything they owned. They did it anyway. Some archaeologists have suggested the logic may run backwards from what we assume: perhaps we did not invent farming and then get bread. Perhaps we wanted bread — and beer, for which there is suggestive Natufian residue — badly enough to invent farming. The loaf, in other words, may be one of the reasons civilization happened. Every time you tear into warm bread, you are performing a gesture older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel, older than every nation and every scripture on earth. The gesture has outlasted almost everything.

---

Trees play the longest game of any individual lives. In the White Mountains of California, at altitudes where the growing season shrinks to a few giddy weeks of summer, grow the Great Basin bristlecone pines — gnarled, half-dead-looking, sculpted by wind into shapes more like driftwood or antlers than trees. One of them, called Methuselah, germinated around 2830 BC, give or take. It was already two centuries old when the Great Pyramid at Giza was finished. It had been alive for roughly two thousand years when the stories of the Trojan War began to be sung. Everything we call ancient history — Sumer, Akkad, Egypt, Greece, Rome — happened during the lifetime of this single organism. It is still alive now, on a slope whose trail is public but whose champion is left deliberately unmarked, out of a well-founded fear of souvenir hunters. There are rumors of older trees — an unnamed bristlecone, a giant Patagonian cypress — but Methuselah holds the verified crown.

The fear is well founded because of what happened to Methuselah's older sibling. In 1964, on Wheeler Peak in Nevada, a graduate student named Donald Currey was studying bristlecones as climate archives when his coring tool jammed in a tree known afterward as Prometheus. With the Forest Service's permission, the tree was cut down so the rings could be counted from a cross-section. When the counting was done, the number came back close to 4,900. Prometheus had been, as far as anyone knew, the oldest non-clonal living thing on Earth. The stump is still there. The story is usually told as a parable, and it is hard to tell it any other way: we met the oldest individual life we have ever found, and we cut it down to find out how old it was.

The bristlecones hold a secret that is almost a philosophy. They live so long precisely because their lives are so hard. The cold, thin, alkaline soil discourages competitors and pests; the slow growth packs the wood dense and resinous, nearly immune to rot; and when parts of the tree die — as most of any old bristlecone has — a narrow ribbon of living bark keeps one strip of crown alive, a lifeboat launched from the wreck of the ship. They survive by austerity, by slow time, by letting most of themselves go. It is not a bad recipe.

---

But "oldest individual" needs an asterisk, because some lives refuse to stay inside one body. In south-central Utah, above Fish Lake, there is a forest that is also a single tree. Pando — Latin for "I spread" — is a quaking aspen that has cloned itself across some 106 acres: roughly 47,000 trunks, all genetically identical, all joined by one root system, together weighing around 6,000 metric tons, which may make it the heaviest known organism on the planet. Each trunk lives a century or so and is replaced; the organism goes on. How long has it gone on? No one knows, and the estimates are dizzying — from 14,000 years to 80,000 or more. Pando may have been spreading across that hillside since before the last ice age ended. Right now it is struggling: deer and cattle eat every young shoot, so the colony is all middle age and no youth. Conservationists have fenced parts of it, and where the fences hold, the children return.

Tasmania keeps an even older quiet thing. King's lomatia is a glossy-leaved shrub, a sterile triploid that cannot make seeds and exists only as cuttings of itself. Radiocarbon dating of fossilized leaves identical to the living plant puts the clone's age around 43,600 years. It was ancient when the glaciers reached their greatest extent. Today only a few hundred stems remain in a single hidden gully, watched over like the last pages of a book.

Under the Mediterranean, off Formentera, grow meadows of Neptune grass that clone themselves by slow horizontal growth — a few centimeters a year. Geneticists who sampled the meadows concluded that some may be tens of thousands of years old, perhaps on the order of a hundred thousand, though the margin of error is wide. If the higher estimates hold, there is seagrass in that bright water that was growing when Neanderthals walked the coasts of Europe. These lives ask you to revise your vocabulary. What is an individual? What is a lifespan? A hundred thousand years measured not in heartbeats but in repetitions — the same green thought, thought again and again.

---

Living things are not the only things that clone themselves. Stories do too, jumping from mind to mind across the centuries, and some of them may be almost inconceivably old. The oldest written texts are infants — the Epic of Gilgamesh assembled some four thousand years ago, the Rigveda composed aloud a bit over three. But writing is just the newest storage medium. Before it there was memory, trained and drilled and armed with technique, and there are reasons to take its reach seriously. In 2015, the geographer Patrick Nunn and the linguist Nicholas Reid examined Aboriginal Australian narratives of coastal drowning — stories, told by communities around the continent, of places that were once land and are now sea: hunting grounds under Spencer Gulf, the time when you could walk to Kangaroo Island, the flooding of the plain that became Port Phillip Bay. Matching the stories to the geological record of post-ice-age sea-level rise, they argued that some of these narratives describe events of seven to ten thousand years ago. If they are right — and the specificity of the matches is eerie — then these stories have been told, night after night, for more than three hundred generations. Songlines bind narrative to landscape, so that the country itself becomes the memory palace; ceremony acts as error-correction. Still, the discipline required staggers. Three hundred generations of getting it right.

Then there is the possibility that a story could be older than that by an order of magnitude. All over the world, the star cluster we call the Pleiades is known as seven sisters — in Greek myth, in Aboriginal Australian traditions, in the legends of the Kiowa — yet almost everyone who looks up can count only six bright stars. The astronomers Ray and Barnaby Norris have suggested a tantalizing explanation: a hundred thousand years ago, the stars Atlas and Pleione would have appeared to the naked eye as a single point of light. Seven visible sisters then;

**Still Here: On the Oldest Things in the World**

Opening:

Sometime around 12,400 BC, in what is now northeastern Jordan, someone baked bread. We know this because in 2018, archaeologists sifting through the remains of a stone fireplace at a site called Shubayqa 1 found charred crumbs — tiny blackened fragments of flatbread, analyzed under an electron microscope until their ingredients could be named: flour ground from wild wheat and barley, mixed with the pulverized tubers of a wetland sedge called club-rush. The bread was unleavened, probably cooked on hot stones or in the ashes. And here is the fact that stops you: it was baked more than four thousand years before anyone, anywhere, had planted a field. The people at Shubayqa were hunter-gatherers, Natufians, who hunted gazelle and gathered what the land offered. Agriculture had not been invented. Villages barely existed. Writing was ten thousand years in the future. And yet there was bread.

Think about what that means. Gathering wild grasses seed by seed, grinding them between stones, mashing tubers, mixing, shaping, baking — it is an enormous amount of labor for a band of people who carried everything they owned. They did it anyway. Some archaeologists have suggested the logic may run backwards from what we assume: perhaps we did not invent farming and then get bread. Perhaps we wanted bread — and beer, which may be even older in desire if not in evidence — badly enough to invent farming. The loaf, in other words, may be one of the reasons civilization happened. Every time you tear into warm bread, you are performing a gesture at least 14,400 years old, older than pottery is not... [careful] — older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel, older than every nation and every scripture on earth. The gesture has outlasted almost everything.

Trees play the longest game of any individuals. In the White Mountains of California, at altitudes where the growing season shrinks to a few giddy weeks of summer, grow the Great Basin bristlecone pines — gnarled, half-dead-looking, sculpted by wind into shapes that seem more like driftwood or antlers than trees. One of them, called Methuselah, germinated around 2830 BC, give or take. It was already two centuries old when the Great Pyramid at Giza was finished. It had been alive for roughly two thousand years when the stories of the Trojan War began to be sung. Everything we call ancient history — Sumer, Akkad, Egypt, Greece, Rome — happened during the lifetime of this single organism. It is still alive now, on a slope the Forest Service declines to identify precisely, out of a well-founded fear of souvenir hunters.

The fear is well founded because of what happened to Methuselah's older sibling. In 1964, on Wheeler Peak in Nevada, a graduate student named Donald Currey was studying bristlecones as climate archives when his coring tool jammed in a tree known afterward as Prometheus. With the Forest Service's permission, the tree was cut down so the rings could be counted from a cross-section. When the counting was done, the number came back close to 4,900. Prometheus had been, as far as anyone knew, the oldest non-clonal living thing on Earth. The stump is still there. The story is usually told as a parable, and it is hard to tell it any other way: we met the oldest individual life we have ever found, and we cut it down to find out how old it was.

The bristlecones hold a secret that is almost a philosophy. They live so long precisely because their lives are so hard. The cold, thin, alkaline soil discourages competitors and pests; the slow growth packs the wood dense and resinous, nearly immune to rot; and when parts of the tree die — as most of any old bristlecone has — a narrow ribbon of living bark keeps one strip of crown alive, a lifeboat launched from the wreck of the ship. They survive by austerity, by slow time, by letting most of themselves go. It is not a bad recipe.

But "oldest individual" needs an asterisk, because some lives refuse to stay inside one body. In south-central Utah, on a slope above Fish Lake, there is a forest that is also a single tree. Pando — Latin for "I spread" — is a quaking aspen that has cloned itself across some 106 acres: roughly 47,000 trunks, all genetically identical, all joined by one root system, together weighing around 6,000 metric tons, which may make it the heaviest known organism on the planet. Pando may have been spreading across that hillside since before the last ice age ended. Right now it is struggling: deer and cattle eat every young shoot, so the colony is all middle age and no youth. Conservationists have fenced parts of it, and where the fences hold, the children return.

Tasmania keeps an even older quiet thing. King's lomatia is a glossy-leaved shrub, a sterile triploid that cannot make seeds and exists only as cuttings of itself. Radiocarbon dating of fossilized leaves identical to the living plant puts the clone's age around 43,600 years. It was ancient when the glaciers reached their greatest extent. Today only a few hundred stems remain in a single hidden gully, watched over like the last pages of a book.

Under the Mediterranean, off Formentera, grow meadows of Neptune grass, Posidonia oceanica, that clone themselves by slow horizontal growth — a few centimeters a year. Geneticists who sampled the meadows concluded that some may be tens of thousands of years old, perhaps on the order of a hundred thousand, though the margin of error is wide. If the higher estimates hold, there is seagrass in that bright water that was growing when Neanderthals walked the coast of Europe. These lives ask you to revise your vocabulary. Section 4 — stories:

Living things are not the only things that clone themselves. Stories do too, jumping from mind to mind across the centuries, and some of them may be almost inconceivably old. The oldest written texts are babies — the Epic of Gilgamesh assembled some four thousand years ago, the Rigveda composed aloud a bit over three. But writing is just the newest storage medium. Before it, there was memory, trained and drilled and armed with technique, and there are reasons to take its reach seriously. In 2015, the geographer Patrick Nunn and the linguist Nicholas Reid examined Aboriginal Australian narratives of coastal drowning — stories, told by communities around the continent, of places that were once land and are now sea: kangaroo hunting grounds under Spencer Gulf, the time when you could walk to Kangaroo Island, the flooding of the plain that became Port Phillip Bay. Matching the stories to the geological record of post-ice-age sea-level rise, they argued that some of these narratives describe events of seven to ten thousand years ago. If they are right — and the specificity of the matches is eerie — then these stories have been told, night after night, for more than three hundred generations. Songlines bind narrative to landscape so that the country itself becomes the memory palace; initiation and ceremony act as error-correction. Still, the discipline required staggers. Three hundred generations of getting it right.

Then there is the possibility that a story could be older than that by an order of magnitude. All over the world, the star cluster we call the Pleiades is known as seven sisters — in Greek myth, in Aboriginal Australian traditions, in the legends of the Kiowa — yet almost everyone who looks up can count only six bright stars. Astronomers Ray and Barnaby Norris have suggested a tantalizing explanation: a hundred thousand years ago, the stars Atlas and Pleione would have appeared to the naked eye as a single point of light. Seven visible sisters then; six now. The hypothesis is speculative, perhaps unfalsifiable, and should be handled like a butterfly wing. But consider what it proposes: that a story told tonight around a fire might have been carried out of Africa, that its first telling predates not just writing and farming but most of the human adventure, and that the "lost sister" has been mourned for a hundred thousand years.

Section 5 — music:

If stories are old, music may be older. In the Hohle Fels cave in Germany's Swabian Jura, archaeologists found, in sediment dated to about 40,000 years ago, a flute carved from the wing bone of a griffon vulture — five finger holes, a V-shaped notch at one end. Replicas play; the notes come out clear and soft. Someone in the deep Ice Age, in a world of mammoths and cave lions, sat in firelight and made music. (A bone from Slovenia, the so-called Divje Babe flute, might be a Neanderthal instrument tens of thousands of years older — or might be a bear femur chewed by hyenas. Science is still arguing.) Music leaves almost no fossil trace; flutes are nearly all that survives. It is safe to assume the singing started long before the instruments.

The oldest song we can actually attempt to play is younger: a clay tablet from the city of Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, inscribed around 1400 BC with a hymn to a goddess and a set of instructions — the strings, the intervals — that scholars read as musical notation. The Hurrian Hymn, it is called, and if you search for it you can hear people playing their best reconstructions: strange, plangent, half-guesswork. And then there is the one that survives complete. Somewhere between roughly 200 BC and 100 AD, near the town of Tralles in what is now Turkey, a man named Seikilos had a marble column engraved with an epitaph — for a woman named Euterpe, probably his wife, and then, it seems, for himself. Along with the words he had the melody inscribed above them, in the notation of the time, and a line that translates as: "I am a tombstone, an image; Seikilos placed me here, an everlasting sign of deathless remembrance." It worked. The stone surfaced in the nineteenth century, and the Seikilos epitaph is now the oldest complete song in the world, words and music together. You can listen to it tonight. The lyric is four lines long, and it is not what you expect an epitaph to say. It says: While you live, shine. Have no grief at all. Life exists only a short while, and time demands its due.

The artifacts tell the same story from another angle: the people of the deep past were not sketches of us. They were us, fully. In a German cave in 1939, excavators found fragments of mammoth ivory that, pieced together over decades, became the Lion Man — a standing figure, about a foot tall, with a human body and the head of a cave lion, carved some 40,000 years ago. It is among the oldest uncontested works of figurative art, and it deserves a pause: it depicts something that does not exist. Whoever made it — experimenters estimate it took hundreds of hours — could hold a fiction in mind and carve it into the world. That is the signature of a mind like ours, and perhaps of religion, or story, or both.

In the Chauvet cave in France, sealed by a rockfall for more than twenty thousand years until 1994, the walls carry lions, rhinos, horses in red and black, painted about 36,000 years ago; torch marks stripe the stone where someone, long ago, rubbed off the charcoal to relight the flame. In one chamber run the footprints of a child, and beside them the prints of a large canid — a wolf, or an early dog, walking with the child through the dark. The most touching mark of all is the oldest and the simplest: the hand stencil. From Sulawesi, where hand stencils go back at least 40,000 years, to Spain, to Argentina's Cueva de las Manos, people pressed a palm to the rock and blew pigment around it. The gesture needs no translation. It says the one thing every human being has always wanted to say: I was here.

And then there is the man himself, who came out of the ice. In 1991, hikers in the Alps on the Austrian-Italian border found a body melting out of a glacier — not, as first assumed, a lost mountaineer, but a man who had died around 5,300 years ago, about 3230 BC. Ötzi, they called him. He was about forty-five, old for his time. He had an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder; he had been murdered, or at least shot in the back, on a mountain pass. He had sixty-one tattoos, mostly lines and crosses, many of them over joints and along the spine in places that ache — possibly treatment for pain, an alpine echo of acupuncture. His last meal was ibex meat and einkorn wheat. He carried a copper axe, a fire-starting kit, and a medicinal fungus. In his genome, researchers found the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, and the markers of lactose intolerance, and the beginnings of heart disease. The tenderness of the details undoes you. This is not a specimen. This is a man with a sore back and a packed lunch, who went up the mountain one day five thousand years ago and did not come down.

Step back, and the pattern in all this survival is worth naming, because it is not the pattern you might expect. The oldest things do not survive by being hard, or by standing still. The bristlecone survives by letting most of itself die; the aspen and the seagrass survive by endlessly becoming new tissue, persistence through replacement; the song survives only when it is sung; the bread survives only by being baked again each morning. Continuity, at these depths, is not the persistence of stuff. It is the persistence of pattern — information outliving matter, the way a wave outlives its water. We flatter ourselves that this is a new idea, but we are made of it: your cells turn over, your atoms swap out, and what persists of you is the pattern. Heraclitus said you cannot step into the same river twice. He might have added that the river is exactly the kind of thing that lasts forever.

There is something else, too, and it is easy to miss: this depth of past is itself a recent discovery. For nearly all of human history, people assumed the world was a few thousand years old. Geology cracked that open only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; radiocarbon dating arrived in the 1940s. The people who baked at Shubayqa could not have known how old their own story would turn out to be; neither, until lately, could anyone. We are among the first generations to be able to look straight down the well of time and see the bottom glinting. To know that a tree predates the pyramids, that a story may predate the human arrival in Australia — wait, no: the stories about sea level rise are by people in Australia... careful. Rephrase: "that a song can be carried across two thousand years intact" — that knowledge is new, and it changes the scale of what a human life is a part of.

**Still Here: On the Oldest Things in the World**

Opening:

Sometime around 12,400 BC, in what is now northeastern Jordan, someone baked bread. We know this because in 2018, archaeologists sifting through the remains of a stone fireplace at a site called Shubayqa 1 found charred crumbs — tiny blackened fragments of flatbread, analyzed under an electron microscope until their ingredients could be named: flour ground from wild wheat and barley, mixed with the pulverized tubers of a wetland sedge called club-rush. The bread was unleavened, probably cooked on hot stones or in the ashes. And here is the fact that stops you: it was baked more than four thousand years before anyone, anywhere, had planted a field. The people at Shubayqa were hunter-gatherers, Natufians, who hunted gazelle and gathered what the land offered. Agriculture had not been invented. Villages barely existed. Writing was ten thousand years in the future. And yet there was bread.

Think about what that means. Gathering wild grasses seed by seed, grinding them between stones, mashing tubers, mixing, shaping, baking — it is an enormous amount of labor for a band of people who carried everything they owned. They did it anyway. Some archaeologists have suggested the logic may run backwards from what we assume: perhaps we did not invent farming and then get bread. Perhaps we wanted bread — and beer, which may be even older in desire if not in evidence — badly enough to invent farming. The loaf, in other words, may be one of the reasons civilization happened. Every time you tear into warm bread, you are performing a gesture at least 14,400 years old, older than pottery is not... [careful] — older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel, older than every nation and every scripture on earth. The gesture has outlasted almost everything.

Section 2 — trees:

Trees play the longest game of any individuals. In the White Mountains of California, at altitudes where the growing season shrinks to a few giddy weeks of summer, grow the Great Basin bristlecone pines — gnarled, half-dead-looking, sculpted by wind into shapes that seem more like driftwood or antlers than trees. One of them, called Methuselah, germinated around 2830 BC, give or take. It was already two centuries old when the Great Pyramid at Giza was finished. It had been alive for roughly two thousand years when the stories of the Trojan War began to be sung. Everything we call ancient history — Sumer, Akkad, Egypt, Greece, Rome — happened during the lifetime of this single organism. It is still alive now, on a slope the Forest Service declines to identify precisely, out of a well-founded fear of souvenir hunters.

The fear is well founded because of what happened to Methuselah's older sibling. In 1964, on Wheeler Peak in Nevada, a graduate student named Donald Currey was studying bristlecones as climate archives when his coring tool jammed in a tree known afterward as Prometheus. With the Forest Service's permission, the tree was cut down so the rings could be counted from a cross-section. When the counting was done, the number came back close to 4,900. Prometheus had been, as far as anyone knew, the oldest non-clonal living thing on Earth. The stump is still there. The story is usually told as a parable, and it is hard to tell it any other way: we met the oldest individual life we have ever found, and we cut it down to find out how old it was.

The bristlecones hold a secret that is almost a philosophy. They live so long precisely because their lives are so hard. The cold, thin, alkaline soil discourages competitors and pests; the slow growth packs the wood dense and resinous, nearly immune to rot; and when parts of the tree die — as most of any old bristlecone has — a narrow ribbon of living bark keeps one strip of crown alive, a lifeboat launched from the wreck of the ship. They survive by austerity, by slow time, by letting most of themselves go. It is not a bad recipe.

Section 3 — clones:

But "oldest individual" needs an asterisk, because some lives refuse to stay inside one body. In south-central Utah, on a slope above Fish Lake, there is a forest that is also a single tree. Pando — Latin for "I spread" — is a quaking aspen that has cloned itself across some 106 acres: roughly 47,000 trunks, all genetically identical, all joined by one root system, together weighing around 6,000 metric tons, which may make it the heaviest known organism on the planet. Each trunk lives a century or so and is replaced; the organism goes on. How long has it gone on? No one knows, and the estimates are dizzying — from 14,000 years to 80,000 or more. Pando may have been spreading across that hillside since before the last ice age ended. Right now it is struggling: deer and cattle eat every young shoot, so the colony is all middle age and no youth. Conservationists have fenced parts of it, and where the fences hold, the children return.

Tasmania keeps an even older quiet thing. King's lomatia is a glossy-leaved shrub, a sterile triploid that cannot make seeds and exists only as cuttings of itself. Radiocarbon dating of fossilized leaves identical to the living plant puts the clone's age around 43,600 years. It was ancient when the glaciers reached their greatest extent. Today only a few hundred stems remain in a single hidden gully, watched over like the last pages of a book.

Under the Mediterranean, off Formentera, grow meadows of Neptune grass, Posidonia oceanica, that clone themselves by slow horizontal growth — a few centimeters a year. Geneticists who sampled the meadows concluded that some may be tens of thousands of years old, perhaps on the order of a hundred thousand, though the margin of error is wide. If the higher estimates hold, there is seagrass in that bright water that was growing when Neanderthals walked the coast of Europe. These lives ask you to revise your vocabulary. What is an individual? What is a lifespan? A hundred thousand years measured not in heartbeats but in repetitions — the same green thought, thought again and again and again.

Section 4 — stories:

Living things are not the only things that clone themselves. Stories do too, jumping from mind to mind across the centuries, and some of them may be almost inconceivably old. The oldest written texts are babies — the Epic of Gilgamesh assembled some four thousand years ago, the Rigveda composed aloud a bit over three. But writing is just the newest storage medium. Before it, there was memory, trained and drilled and armed with technique, and there are reasons to take its reach seriously. In 2015, the geographer Patrick Nunn and the linguist Nicholas Reid examined Aboriginal Australian narratives of coastal drowning — stories, told by communities around the continent, of places that were once land and are now sea: kangaroo hunting grounds under Spencer Gulf, the time when you could walk to Kangaroo Island, the flooding of the plain that became Port Phillip Bay. Matching the stories to the geological record of post-ice-age sea-level rise, they argued that some of these narratives describe events of seven to ten thousand years ago. If they are right — and the specificity of the matches is eerie — then these stories have been told, night after night, for more than three hundred generations. Songlines bind narrative to landscape so that the country itself becomes the memory palace; initiation and ceremony act as error-correction. Still, the discipline required staggers. Three hundred generations of getting it right.

Then there is the possibility that a story could be older than that by an order of magnitude. All over the world, the star cluster we call the Pleiades is known as seven sisters — in Greek myth, in Aboriginal Australian traditions, in the legends of the Kiowa — yet almost everyone who looks up can count only six bright stars. Astronomers Ray and Barnaby Norris have suggested a tantalizing explanation: a hundred thousand years ago, the stars Atlas and Pleione would have appeared to the naked eye as a single point of light. Seven visible sisters then; six now. The hypothesis is speculative, perhaps unfalsifiable, and should be handled like a butterfly wing. But consider what it proposes: that a story told tonight around a fire might have been carried out of Africa, that its first telling predates not just writing and farming but most of the human adventure, and that the "lost sister" has been mourned for a hundred thousand years.

Section 5 — music:

If stories are old, music may be older. In the Hohle Fels cave in Germany's Swabian Jura, archaeologists found, in sediment dated to about 40,000 years ago, a flute carved from the wing bone of a griffon vulture — five finger holes, a V-shaped notch at one end. Replicas play; the notes come out clear and soft. Someone in the deep Ice Age, in a world of mammoths and cave lions, sat in firelight and made music. (A bone from Slovenia, the so-called Divje Babe flute, might be a Neanderthal instrument tens of thousands of years older — or might be a bear femur chewed by hyenas. Science is still arguing.) Music leaves almost no fossil trace; flutes are nearly all that survives. It is safe to assume the singing started long before the instruments.

The oldest song we can actually attempt to play is younger: a clay tablet from the city of Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, inscribed around 1400 BC with a hymn to a goddess and a set of instructions — the strings, the intervals — that scholars read as musical notation. The Hurrian Hymn, it is called, and if you search for it you can hear people playing their best reconstructions: strange, plangent, half-guesswork. And then there is the one that survives complete. Somewhere between roughly 200 BC and 100 AD, near the town of Tralles in what is now Turkey, a man named Seikilos had a marble column engraved with an epitaph — for a woman named Euterpe, probably his wife, and then, it seems, for himself. Along with the words he had the melody inscribed above them, in the notation of the time, and a line that translates as: "I am a tombstone, an image; Seikilos placed me here, an everlasting sign of deathless remembrance." It worked. The stone surfaced in the nineteenth century, and the Seikilos epitaph is now the oldest complete song in the world, words and music together. You can listen to it tonight. The lyric is four lines long, and it is not what you expect an epitaph to say. It says: While you live, shine. Have no grief at all. Life exists only a short while, and time demands its due.

Section 6 — objects/bodies:

The artifacts tell the same story from another angle: the people of the deep past were not sketches of us. They were us, fully. In a German cave in 1939, excavators found fragments of mammoth ivory that, pieced together over decades, became the Lion Man — a standing figure, about a foot tall, with a human body and the head of a cave lion, carved some 40,000 years ago. It is among the oldest uncontested works of figurative art, and it deserves a pause: it depicts something that does not exist. Whoever made it — experimenters estimate it took hundreds of hours — could hold a fiction in mind and carve it into the world. That is the signature of a mind like ours, and perhaps of religion, or story, or both.

In the Chauvet cave in France, sealed by a rockfall for more than twenty thousand years until 1994, the walls carry lions, rhinos, horses in red and black, painted about 36,000 years ago; torch marks stripe the stone where someone, long ago, rubbed off the charcoal to relight the flame. In one chamber run the footprints of a child, and beside them the prints of a large canid — a wolf, or an early dog, walking with the child through the dark. The most touching mark of all is the oldest and the simplest: the hand stencil. From Sulawesi, where hand stencils go back at least 40,000 years, to Spain, to Argentina's Cueva de las Manos, people pressed a palm to the rock and blew pigment around it. The gesture needs no translation. It says the one thing every human being has always wanted to say: I was here.

And then there is the man himself, who came out of the ice. In 1991, hikers in the Alps on the Austrian-Italian border found a body melting out of a glacier — not, as first assumed, a lost mountaineer, but a man who had died around 5,300 years ago, about 3230 BC. Ötzi, they called him. He was about forty-five, old for his time. He had an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder; he had been murdered, or at least shot in the back, on a mountain pass. He had sixty-one tattoos, mostly lines and crosses, many of them over joints and along the spine in places that ache — possibly treatment for pain, an alpine echo of acupuncture. His last meal was ibex meat and einkorn wheat. He carried a copper axe, a fire-starting kit, and a medicinal fungus. In his genome, researchers found the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, and the markers of lactose intolerance, and the beginnings of heart disease. The tenderness of the details undoes you. This is not a specimen. This is a man with a sore back and a packed lunch, who went up the mountain one day five thousand years ago and did not come down.

Section 7 — synthesis (keep ~250):

Step back, and the pattern in all this survival is worth naming, because it is not the pattern you might expect. The oldest things do not survive by being hard, or by standing still. The bristlecone survives by letting most of itself die; the aspen and the seagrass survive by endlessly becoming new tissue, persistence through replacement; the song survives only when it is sung; the bread survives only by being baked again each morning. Continuity, at these depths, is not the persistence of stuff. It is the persistence of pattern — information outliving matter, the way a wave outlives its water. We flatter ourselves that this is a new idea, but we are made of it: your cells turn over, your atoms swap out, and what persists of you is the pattern. Heraclitus said you cannot step into the same river twice. He might have added that the river is exactly the kind of thing that lasts forever.

There is something else, too, and it is easy to miss: this depth of past is itself a recent discovery. For nearly all of human history, people assumed the world was a few thousand years old. Geology cracked that open only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; radiocarbon dating arrived in the 1940s. The people who baked at Shubayqa could not have known how old their own story would turn out to be; neither, until lately, could anyone. We are among the first generations to be able to look straight down the well of time and see the bottom glinting. To know that a tree predates the pyramids, that a story may predate the human arrival in Australia — wait, no: the stories about sea level rise are by people in Australia... careful. Rephrase: "that a song can be carried across two thousand years intact" — that knowledge is new, and it changes the scale of what a human life is a part of.
